opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the games story is actually really instructive, and it's worth being precise about why.

If you look at something like Go, for a long time people said it was the kind of thing that required intuition, taste, a sort of human feel for the board. The search space is enormous, so you can't just brute-force it. And what we learned with systems like AlphaGo, and then AlphaZero, is that if you have two ingredients, you can get superhuman performance. The first is a way to generate a huge number of attempts, which is search guided by a learned model that develops something like intuition. The second is a clean, reliable signal telling you whether you won or lost. Once you have that verifier, the system can play against itself, learn from its mistakes, and keep improving well past where any human was.

Mathematics has a lot of that same structure. A proof is either correct or it isn't. Especially with formal systems like Lean, you can mechanically check whether an argument goes through. That's the reward signal. And the space of possible proofs is vast, like the space of Go games, so you need learned intuition about which directions are promising. That's the part language models and reinforcement learning have been getting good at.

So when I look at math through that lens, it looks much more like a game than like a fuzzy, open-ended domain where it's hard to tell whether you've succeeded. That's the source of my optimism. In domains where we can verify answers, we've repeatedly seen these systems go from "can't do it at all" to "better than the best humans" faster than people expected.

There are real caveats. Choosing which problems are interesting, building good definitions, knowing which theorem is worth proving: that's harder to put into a win/loss signal, and it's where much of the deep creativity in math lives. But even there, as a physicist, my instinct is that a lot of what we call taste is accumulated experience with what works, and that's exactly what these systems are good at absorbing. So I wouldn't bet against them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that people sometimes miss about games is that Go, chess, these are actually hard problems in a very particular sense. The search space is enormous, far bigger than you could ever brute-force, and the only way to make progress is to develop something like intuition. You have to learn which moves are worth considering and which ones to prune, and then you have to combine that intuition with the ability to look ahead and verify that a line actually works.

And when you describe it that way, that's basically what a mathematician does. You have an enormous space of possible proof steps, you can't enumerate them, and the whole skill is in having a sense of where the interesting direction is, and then checking rigorously that the step you took is actually valid. Mathematics has this wonderful property, the same one games have, which is that you get a clean signal at the end. In Go, you either won or you lost. In math, the proof either goes through or it doesn't. You can formalize it, run it through a proof checker, and get a definitive yes or no.

That verifiability is really the key ingredient. The reason self-play worked so well for AlphaGo is that the system could generate its own experience and the environment told it, unambiguously, whether it was getting better. Lots of domains don't have that. If you're trying to get better at writing essays or at being a doctor, the feedback is noisy, slow, and often subjective. But in math, with formal systems like Lean, you have a referee that never gets tired and is never wrong. So the recipe that worked in games, where you combine a learned intuition with search and a verifier, actually transfers, and we've already started to see that with systems reaching olympiad-level performance.

The other reason I'm optimistic is that games taught us that these systems don't just imitate humans, they can find things humans didn't see. Move 37 was the famous example. Human players had been playing Go for thousands of years and there was still this move that looked wrong to everyone and turned out to be brilliant. Mathematics is thousands of years old too, and I'd be genuinely surprised if there weren't analogous moves sitting there, ideas that don't look natural to a human-trained mind but that open things up. So I don't think of it as "AI will do the math we already know how to do faster." I think the games result is evidence that there might be genuinely new mathematics that these systems help us find.

astra-6.text:
Well, games show us that AI can do more than reproduce strategies people have already discovered. It can find moves that surprise even the best human players, and those moves can turn out to reveal something new about the game.

Mathematics has some of that same structure. You have rules, you have a vast space of possible moves, and you’re trying to find a sequence that gets you somewhere interesting. Checking a proof can be much easier than finding it, so there’s an opportunity to explore creatively while still having a rigorous way to check the result.

Of course, mathematics is much more open-ended. You don’t always know what the right question is, let alone what winning looks like. So success at games doesn’t establish that mathematical discovery will follow. But it gives us a reason to think that a system can learn to navigate an enormous space of possibilities and develop strategies that go beyond our own intuition. That’s what makes me optimistic.

sol-6.1.text:
Games show us that AI can do more than reproduce strategies people already know. It can explore a huge space of possibilities and discover moves that surprise even the best human players. Mathematics has some of that same character: you have a set of rules, but the consequences of those rules can be extraordinarily rich.

Of course, finding interesting mathematics is harder to specify than winning a game. You need to decide which questions are worth asking, and a proof has to hold up to scrutiny. But the game results suggest that human intuition isn’t the ceiling. If we can give these systems useful feedback and ways to check their reasoning, there’s reason to hope they’ll help us discover mathematical ideas we wouldn’t have found on our own.
